title: Etoposide-induced angina in a patient with small cell lung carcinoma: a case report.
abstract: Background The combination of cisplatin and etoposide is a standard therapy for small cell lung cancer; however, ischemic heart disease is a known complication. We report a rare case of effort angina pectoris that worsened during initial treatment of small cell lung cancer with etoposide. Case presentation A 73-year-old Asian male was admitted to our hospital with effort angina. Coronary angiography revealed severe stenosis with significant calcification of the proximal right coronary artery. Computed tomography revealed a 21-mm-sized nodule in the right upper lobe and hilar lymphadenopathy suggestive of lung cancer. The patient underwent thoracoscopic wedge resection before coronary revascularization, and intraoperative findings indicated a small cell carcinoma with hilar lymph node metastases. Early postoperative definitive treatment consisting of chemotherapy with cisplatin plus etoposide and accelerated hyperfractionated radiation was planned. During the first chemotherapy session, on postoperative day 7, the patient complained of chest pain, and an electrocardiogram showed slight ST depression in leads V5 and V6 while receiving etoposide; nitroglycerin improved his symptoms. Although treatment was resumed with the administration of nicorandil the next day, the same symptoms were observed during the infusion of etoposide. Accordingly, chemoradiation therapy was suspended and revascularization of the right coronary artery was performed. Etoposide and cisplatin were readministered 3 days after revascularization, without any chest symptoms. Conclusion Chemotherapy for malignant tumors carries the risk of progression to coronary artery disease. To prevent serious ischemic events, sufficient discussions between oncologists and cardiologists and careful observation of chest symptoms are needed.

title: Very late local recurrence of chromophobe renal cell carcinoma 15 years after nephrectomy: a case report.
abstract: Background Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (chRCC) is a rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 5% of cases. Although generally associated with a favorable prognosis, late recurrences may occur. Local recurrence more than a decade after nephrectomy is exceptionally rare, and optimal management remains poorly defined. Case presentation We report a 79-year-old Greek man who underwent radical left nephrectomy and adrenalectomy in 2009 for a 13 × 10 × 9 cm moderately differentiated chRCC, classified in the original pathology report as pT2 pNX pMX, G2, R0. Fifteen years later, he presented with progressive limitation of left hip flexion and increasing constipation. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a solitary 9 × 8 × 7.5 cm left para-aortic retroperitoneal mass without radiologically detectable distant metastatic disease. Biopsy findings were consistent with recurrent renal cell carcinoma. The lesion was clinically classified as a local recurrence based on its location within the previous nephrectomy operative field and the absence of other metastatic lesions, although a solitary metastasis could not be unequivocally excluded histopathologically. After multidisciplinary assessment, complete surgical resection with systematic retroperitoneal lymph-node dissection was performed. Histopathological examination showed morphological features compatible with recurrence or metastasis of the previous chRCC, tumor-free margins, tumor-free sampled peritumoral skeletal muscle, and 0/16 involved lymph nodes. Immunohistochemical analysis was not performed. At 1-year follow-up, the patient remained clinically well with no radiological evidence of local recurrence or distant metastatic disease. Conclusion Very late recurrence of chRCC may occur after a prolonged disease-free interval. In carefully selected patients with isolated and potentially resectable recurrence, complete surgical resection may represent a feasible treatment option within an individualized multidisciplinary approach. The 1-year follow-up in this case is insufficient to establish long-term oncological control, and continued surveillance is warranted.

title: Cell-free DNA-guided detection, surveillance, and therapeutic adaptation for breast cancer.
abstract: Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) analysis provides a minimally invasive approach to breast cancer assessment across early detection, minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring, and treatment adaptation in advanced disease. This review evaluates these applications by distinguishing analytical validity, clinical detection performance, prognostic validity, and clinical utility. In early detection, assays integrating genomic, epigenomic, fragmentomic, and protein-based features have shown encouraging performance in evaluated cohorts; however, sensitivity remains limited in low-burden disease, particularly stage I breast cancer. Their potential clinical role depends on the incremental information they provide beyond established imaging and diagnostic pathways. In the curative-intent setting, circulating tumor DNA detection after treatment is associated with recurrence risk and can precede clinical or radiographic relapse, supporting prognostic stratification and the design of MRD-guided intervention trials. Whether such interventions improve clinical outcomes remains a central unresolved question. In advanced breast cancer, plasma genotyping supports treatment selection in defined molecular contexts. Randomized trials of ESR1 mutation-guided endocrine switching have demonstrated progression-free survival benefits with specific treatment strategies, providing evidence beyond biomarker-outcome associations, although overall survival benefit remains to be established. Across applications, interpretation depends on assay characteristics, molecular input, disease setting, sampling schedule, and the clinical decision being evaluated. Future studies should connect assay performance to patient benefit through comparison with existing care, clinically meaningful endpoints, and assessment of treatment burden and downstream investigations. This approach will help define where cfDNA testing can contribute meaningfully to breast cancer management.

title: Deep learning denoising and deep learning-augmented contrast enhancement improve ultra-high-resolution photon-counting-detector CCTA image quality.
abstract: Objective Ultrahigh-resolution (UHR) coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) using a photon-counting detector (PCD) provides excellent spatial resolution but is limited by increased image noise. We evaluated whether deep learning (DL)-based denoising and contrast enhancement can further improve UHR-CCTA image quality. Materials and methods UHR-CCTA scans from 25 patients with coronary artery disease were retrospectively analyzed. Images were reconstructed at 0.2-mm slice thickness without and with quantum iterative reconstruction (QIR, Q off -Q 4 ), and subsequently processed using a DL tool for denoising and increasing iodine contrast enhancement. Subjective image quality (sharpness, noise, vessel wall delineation, and overall quality) was assessed by three radiologists using a 5-point Likert scale. Objective analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and coronary wall sharpness. Differences between image sets were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results DL-based CCTA demonstrated significantly superior subjective image quality across all parameters compared to standard reconstructions, with an overall median image quality ([interquartile interval, IQR]: 4 [3-5] versus 2 [2-3], p < 0.001). SNR and CNR were significantly higher for DL-based CCTA across all QIR levels (all p < 0.001). The highest values were observed for DL-based CCTAQ 4 versus UHR-CCTAQ 4 (SNR: 258.0 ± 147.5 versus 145.2 ± 50.1; CNR: 25.8 ± 17.1 versus 11.1 ± 4.5; both p < 0.001). Coronary wall sharpness was improved for DL-based CCTA for Q 1-4 (all p < 0.027). Conclusion DL-based denoising and iodine contrast enhancement effectively reduce noise and improve anatomic detail in UHR-CCTA, providing incremental value beyond vendor-specific reconstruction, particularly at high QIR strength levels. Key points Question Deep learning reduces noise and enhances contrast in ultrahigh-resolution coronary CT angiography. Findings Image quality improves beyond standard iterative reconstruction methods, and vessel wall sharpness and diagnostic clarity significantly increase. Relevance statement This study aimed to determine at which levels of vendor-specific iterative reconstruction, DL-based denoising and contrast enhancement perform best in UHR CCTA, providing a foundation for future investigations on how these technical improvements may translate into diagnostic benefits.

title: Image quality and artefact reduction for tantalum clips in ocular proton therapy using photon-counting CT.
abstract: Objective Tantalum fiducials ("clips") used in intraocular proton therapy generate strong artefacts in conventional computed tomography, limiting the visibility of tumours and anatomical structures. This study investigated the potential of photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) for reducing tantalum-related artefacts. Materials and methods Two phantom models containing tantalum clips were examined using a photon-counting CT system and two conventional CT scanners with energy-integrating detectors (EICT). Reconstruction parameters, including tube voltage, image resolution, reconstruction kernel, virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI), and iterative metal artefact reduction (iMAR), were systematically optimised. Image quality was evaluated using objective metrics assessing homogeneity, noise, contrast, structural similarity, and artefact volume, complemented by a blinded subjective observer study. Correlations between objective and subjective results were analysed using Spearman's rank correlation. Results Objectively, PCCT showed no significant advantage over the modern EICT scanner but significantly outperformed the older-generation EICT therapy simulator. In contrast, blinded observers consistently preferred PCCT images. iMAR was the dominant factor influencing image quality. VMI alone did not yield relevant improvements. High-energy VMI (110 keV) combined with iMAR achieved the best subjective ratings. Higher spatial resolution due to smaller voxel sizes showed no clinically relevant benefit for artefact reduction. Soft reconstruction kernels provided the best balance between artefact suppression and image noise. Objective rankings correlated strongly with subjective assessments. Conclusion PCCT combined with iMAR improves subjective image quality in intraocular proton therapy and reduces the perceived severity of tantalum artefacts. Nevertheless, tantalum remains a major challenge in image-guided proton therapy, requiring further optimisation of imaging and reconstruction strategies. Key points Question Photon-counting CT may improve visualisation of tantalum clips and reduce metal artefacts in ocular proton therapy planning compared with conventional CT systems. Findings Photon-counting CT achieved the highest subjective image quality ratings, while iterative metal artefact reduction remained the dominant factor influencing artefact suppression. Relevance statement Photon-counting CT combined with iterative metal artefact reduction can improve visualisation of tantalum clips and surrounding anatomy in ocular proton therapy planning and may support more reliable tumour localisation despite limited objective differences compared with state-of-the-art conventional CT.

title: Time-dependent diffusion MRI in determining mismatch repair status of endometrial cancer.
abstract: Objectives Mismatch repair (MMR) proteins are important in determining therapeutic strategy in endometrial cancer (EC). We investigated the role of microstructural parameters derived from time-dependent diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (td-dMRI) in differentiating MMR status of EC. Materials and methods This prospective single-center study enrolled patients with suspected EC who underwent preoperative td-dMRI. Tumors were classified as MMR-deficient (dMMR) and MMR-proficient (pMMR) by immunohistochemistry. The microstructural parameters, including intracellular volume fraction ( vin ), cell diameter ( d ), cellularity ( ρ ), extracellular diffusivity ( Dex ), and water exchange rate constant ( kin ), were derived by fitting td-dMRI data with three methods (IMPULSED, JOINT, and EXCHANGE), together with the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Differences in these microstructural parameters between dMMR and pMMR EC were compared. The diagnostic performances were evaluated by the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Eighty-two patients (17 dMMR, 61.8 ± 10.1 years and 65 pMMR, 58.6 ± 11.8 years) were recruited. dMMR EC exhibited higher vin , ρ and lower Dex , ADC values than pMMR EC (p ≤ 0.003). IMPULSED and JOINT demonstrated higher AUCs than conventional ADC (p = 0.025 and 0.046, respectively). The combined selected microstructural parameters ( vin and Dex ) derived from JOINT achieved an AUC of 0.903; JOINT demonstrated superior parametric stability and marginally better calibration than IMPULSED. Conclusion In this exploratory study, td-dMRI discriminated between dMMR and pMMR ECs, providing information on the intricate microscopic organizational structures in tumors. The microstructural parameters may serve as a promising method to improve the diagnostic efficacy of diffusion-weighted MRI in differentiating MMR status of EC. Key points Question There remains an unmet need for noninvasive, preoperative tools to assess DNA MMR status in EC. Findings td-dMRI showed significant differences in microstructural parameters between dMMR and pMMR tumors. Relevance statement td-dMRI shows potential as a noninvasive imaging approach for preoperative assessment of MMR status in EC and may support individualized treatment planning.

title: Diagnostic accuracy and reliability of susceptibility map-weighted imaging in patients with clinically uncertain parkinsonian syndromes.
abstract: Objectives Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, accompanied by increased iron accumulation, particularly in the nigrosome-1 subregion. Differentiating neurodegenerative disorders like PD from non-neurodegenerative causes of parkinsonism can be challenging. In clinically uncertain parkinsonian syndrome (CUPS), dopamine transporter (DAT)-single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) can aid diagnosis. However, susceptibility map-weighted imaging (SMWI) provides a promising magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) alternative. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and reliability of visual SMWI assessment by radiologists in CUPS and the added value of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven diagnostic software. Materials and methods Patients with CUPS who underwent DAT-SPECT between January 2019 and July 2023 were included. Four radiologists, blinded to clinical symptoms and diagnosis, visually rated nigrosome-1 on axial SMWI reconstructions as normal, unclear, or abnormal. After the initial assessment, the radiologists re-evaluated the scans with AI-driven software assistance, designed to classify and quantify nigrosome-1 integrity. The reference standard was the final clinical diagnosis incorporating DAT-SPECT results. Results One hundred eighty patients were included (mean age 67.9, range 31-86, 120 males), 84 with neurodegenerative and 96 with non-neurodegenerative parkinsonism. Mean diagnostic accuracy was 80% (range 73-83%), with substantial inter-rater reliability (Fleiss κ 0.65). With software assistance, diagnostic accuracy improved to 87% (range 85-91%), and inter-rater agreement increased to almost perfect (Fleiss κ 0.86). Conclusion SMWI, particularly with AI-driven software assistance, is a promising and accessible MRI-based technique that may support the diagnostic workup in clinically uncertain parkinsonism, aiding the distinction between neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative causes. Key points Question Can susceptibility map-weighted imaging (SMWI) reliably differentiate neurodegenerative from non-neurodegenerative parkinsonism in clinically uncertain cases, and does artificial intelligence (AI)-driven software assistance improve radiologist performance? Findings Visual assessment had an accuracy of 80%, with substantial inter-rater reliability. AI-driven software assistance increased accuracy to 87% and improved inter-rater reliability. Relevance statement SMWI can differentiate neurodegenerative from non-neurodegenerative parkinsonism in clinically uncertain cases and may support the diagnostic process by offering an accessible MRI-based technique, facilitating an efficient diagnostic workup, and enabling early diagnosis in clinically uncertain parkinsonism.

title: High-power radiofrequency ablation with optimized pulsing algorithm for renal tumors: initial clinical experience and safety profile.
abstract: Incidental diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma is increasing. While surgery remains the standard treatment for localized T1b or larger lesions, image-guided percutaneous ablation represents a valid alternative for T1a cases. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is effective but limited by smaller ablation volumes and sensitivity to the heat-sink effect. Microwave ablation and cryoablation have emerged to address these limitations, although the first is susceptible to thermal injury to adjacent structures and the second requires multiple, larger probes and longer procedures. High-power RFA (HP-RFA) is a recent development that delivers higher energy (370 versus 200 W), enabling faster and larger ablations. This study evaluated the feasibility and safety of a novel HP-RFA system incorporating an impedance-controlled pulsed algorithm and internally cooled electrodes. Five patients with small renal tumors (mean diameter 2.3 cm) unsuitable for surgery underwent ultrasound- or computed tomography-guided HP-RFA. Technical success, safety, and early tumor control were assessed. All procedures were technically successful. No major complications occurred; one minor perirenal hematoma was managed conservatively. Follow-up imaging at 6 months demonstrated complete tumor ablation without local recurrence. These preliminary findings suggest that HP-RFA is feasible and safe for treating small renal tumors and may represent a promising evolution of RFA. Further studies are needed. KEY POINTS: Question Can HP-RFA provide feasible and safe minimally invasive treatment for small renal tumors while overcoming limitations of conventional RFA? Findings Technical success and efficacy of HP-RFA were achieved in 100% of cases. No major complications. Complete tumor ablation was accomplished. Relevance statement HP-RFA demonstrates feasibility, safety, and effective early tumor control in small renal tumors. By enabling larger, faster ablations, it may overcome limitations of conventional RFA and expand the employment of minimally invasive treatment options instead of surgical approaches.

title: MRI-based virtual radiographs of the pelvis for assessment of acetabular morphology.
abstract: Objectives We generated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based virtual radiographs (VRs) from hips with/without intra-articular contrast and compared them with conventional anteroposterior pelvic radiographs (CR) regarding measurement bias, interobserver and intraobserver agreement, and diagnosis of acetabular deformities; we also assessed hip deformity prevalence on VR in asymptomatic participants. Materials and methods Retrospective study of 50 patients (100 hips; mean age 34 years) with femoroacetabular impingement or hip dysplasia undergoing CR and unilateral magnetic resonance arthrography. Additionally, 53 asymptomatic participants underwent noncontrast MRI. Segmentation of the osseous pelvis was performed on T1-weighted volume interpolated breathhold examination (VIBE) Dixon MRI using 3D nnU-Net, pseudo-computed tomography generation, and cone-beam projection to generate VR. Acetabular coverage (lateral center edge angle (LCE), acetabular index (AI), anterior/posterior coverage, extrusion index (EI)), and acetabular version were compared between CR and VR. Interobserver agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and κ statistics; bias with Bland-Altman analysis. Results Interobserver agreement for VR ranged from moderate to almost perfect (ICC/κ 0.60-0.94), except for the AI. LCE showed no significant bias with ( - 0.2° ± 2.5, p = 0.663) or without contrast ( - 0.2° ± 2.2, p = 0.530). Systematic differences occurred for AI, EI, anterior/posterior coverage, and ischial spine sign; 57-75% of discrepancies were within CR interobserver variation. Diagnostic classification showed substantial agreement between CR and VR (κ = 0.62), comparable to CR interobserver agreement (κ = 0.70). In asymptomatic participants, 13% had acetabular dysplasia, 68% normal coverage, and 19% overcoverage. Conclusion MRI-based VR provides acetabular morphology assessment comparable to CR and enables radiation-free evaluation in symptomatic patients and asymptomatic populations. Key points Question Can MRI-based virtual radiographs reproduce conventional radiographic measurements of acetabular morphology, enabling radiation-free two-dimensional assessment in symptomatic patients and asymptomatic populations? Findings The lateral center-edge angle showed no significant bias between virtual and conventional radiographs; diagnostic classification of acetabular deformities agreed substantially (κ = 0.62), comparable to conventional radiograph interobserver agreement. Relevance Statement MRI-derived virtual radiographs can provide acetabular measurements comparable to conventional radiographs without ionizing radiation, supporting integration into three-dimensional surgical planning and enabling assessment in young patients and population-based cohorts where repeated radiographs are undesirable.

title: Oxygen-enhanced brain MRI using dynamic gradient-echo and MR fingerprinting.
abstract: Objectives Oxygen-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using dynamic three-dimensional (3D) gradient-echo and MR fingerprinting (MRF) was applied to evaluate oxygen transit from blood to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Materials and methods Twenty healthy participants, enrolled between December 2023 and March 2024, underwent 3-T MRI including Pre-oxygen inhalation 3D MRF (pre-O₂ MRF), dynamic 3D gradient-echo (volumetric interpolated breath-hold examination, VIBE) during oxygen inhalation, and post-oxygen inhalation 3D MRF (post-O₂ MRF). Pre-O₂ and post-O₂ MRF each consisted of two acquisitions. Signal intensity on dynamic VIBE and T1 relaxation times from MRF were evaluated in gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), surface CSF, and ventricles using volumes of interest (VOIs). Results Dynamic 3D VIBE demonstrated a rapid signal increase in surface CSF immediately after oxygen inhalation, with a smaller increase in GM. Post-oxygen inhalation VIBE signal was significantly higher than pre-oxygen inhalation signal in surface CSF (p < 0.001) and GM (p < 0.001). T1 relaxation times differed significantly across phases for GM, WM, and surface CSF (p < 0.001) as well as for ventricles (p = 0.024). Large effect sizes were observed for surface CSF (Cohen dz = 4.15) and GM (Cohen dz = 1.31) in dynamic 3D VIBE, as well as for surface CSF (Cohen f = 1.31) and GM (Cohen f = 0.73) in T1 relaxation time measurement, suggesting substantial physiological changes following oxygen inhalation. Conclusion Dynamic 3D VIBE images visualized oxygen inhalation-related signal change in the surface CSF, which were quantitatively validated by T1 relaxation time reductions derived from 3D MRF. Key points Question Can noninvasive oxygen-enhanced brain MRI visualize and quantify oxygen-related signal changes in cerebrospinal fluid using dynamic 3D gradient-echo and 3D MR fingerprinting? Findings Dynamic 3D gradient-echo showed rapid surface CSF signal increases after oxygen inhalation, accompanied by significant T1 reductions on 3D MR fingerprinting. Relevance statement This noninvasive oxygen-enhanced MR approach may provide a clinically feasible method for assessing oxygen transit into CSF and could support future investigations of human CSF dynamics. Dynamic 3D gradient-echo images visualized oxygen inhalation-related signal change in the surface CSF, which were quantitatively validated by T1 relaxation time reductions derived from 3D MRF.

title: MRI radiomics of pancreatic tumours: a systematic review of methodological quality and imaging reproducibility.
abstract: Objectives Radiomics holds potential for personalised treatment, but reproducibility is hindered by inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters and methodological details. This study aims to identify and evaluate key MR imaging parameters to support radiomics reproducibility and to systematically evaluate the quality of published MRI radiomics studies focused on pancreatic tumours. Materials and methods The literature search was conducted in the Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases. Human studies investigating MRI radiomics in pancreatic tumours were included. An imaging reporting checklist was developed and used to identify and evaluate imaging parameters in eligible studies. The methodological quality score (METRICS) and checklist for evaluation of radiomics research (CLEAR) score were calculated for each study. Results Seventy-eight studies, encompassing 241 MRI pulse sequences (143 anatomical and 98 functional), were included. The imaging checklist identified ten core items as key parameters for ensuring reproducible MRI radiomics. Across all studies, none provided complete or consistent reporting of these parameters, with frequent omissions in imaging acquisition and reconstruction details. Methodological and reporting quality remained suboptimal, reflected by median METRICS and CLEAR scores of 52.4% (45-60%) and 62.3% (56-69%), respectively. Reproducibility and quality of radiomics studies would benefit from clear reporting of imaging parameters, consistent documentation of radiomics settings, and control of confounding variables. Additionally, transparency in model validation, preprocessing, and explanation methods would further enhance reproducibility and clinical relevance. Conclusion A focused imaging reproducibility checklist has been developed, and it has been demonstrated that no pancreatic tumour MRI radiomics study reported all necessary imaging parameters for reproducibility. Methodological and reporting quality on broader radiomics components was also poor, highlighting the potential value of such a checklist for improving standardised reporting in radiomics studies. Key points Question There is inconsistent reporting of imaging parameters across MRI protocols used for pancreatic tumours radiomics analysis. Findings The developed MR imaging reporting checklist provides structured guidelines to promote consistent documentation of MR imaging parameters and support reproducible radiomics research. Relevance statement By identifying how key MR imaging acquisition and reconstruction parameters are currently presented in MRI radiomics studies of pancreatic tumours, this study highlights inconsistencies and omissions in reporting, underscoring the need for more transparent reporting and adherence to guidelines to support radiomics reproducibility.

title: Patient-specific biophysical AI-powered modeling for predicting RFA volumes in HCC.
abstract: Objectives To clinically evaluate a fully automated, artificial intelligence-powered, patient-specific biophysical model for predicting radiofrequency ablation (RFA) volumes in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and to compare its performance with manufacturer-provided ablation estimates. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 96 RFA procedures in 65 HCC patients treated using a single ablation with a cluster needle. Tumors, needle position, and postablation zone were manually segmented on periprocedural computed tomography. Liver parenchyma and vascular structures were automatically extracted using deep learning. A graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated biophysical model simulated heat transfer, vascular heat-sink effects, and tissue necrosis using patient-specific anatomy and procedural data. Correlations between ablation volume manually segmented and clinical or anatomical parameters (ablation time, ablation tip temperature, tumor-capsule distance, vessel proximity, type, and diameter) were assessed. Model-predicted volumes were compared with ground truth and manufacturer estimates using relative volume difference (RVD) and volume similarity. Results Final ablation volumes showed wide variability (7.9-78.8 cm³) and were not correlated with any individual clinical or anatomical parameter (Pearson r - 0.02 to 0.29). Across 94 evaluable cases, simulated and ground-truth volumes were similar (p = 0.165), while manufacturer estimates significantly overestimated ablation volume (p < 0.001). The model achieved a median RVD of 0.39 (interquartile range 0.24-0.57), significantly lower than the manufacturer's algorithm (1.04; 0.64-1.61). Incorporating patient-specific ablation time further improved accuracy. Simulation was fast (0.45 s per second of ablation on GPU). Conclusion A fully automated, patient-specific biophysical model substantially improves RFA ablation volume prediction in HCC compared with manufacturer approximations, supporting its potential role in personalized treatment planning and outcome standardization. Key points Question In patients with hepatocellular carcinoma, can a fully automated, AI-powered, patient-specific biophysical model predict radiofrequency ablation volume more accurately than manufacturer-provided estimates? Findings A fully automated, AI-powered biophysical model integrating patient-specific anatomy and vasculature predicted RFA volume significantly better than manufacturer estimates (median relative volume difference (RVD) 0.39 versus 1.04). Relevance statement Accurate ablation volume prediction could support personalized radiofrequency ablation (RFA) planning, reduce reliance on operator experience, and standardize treatment margins in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), potentially improving local tumor control and reducing recurrence in cirrhotic patients undergoing thermal ablation.

title: Assessment of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease severity using deep learning-based kidney volumetry in CT.
abstract: Objectives Accurate quantification of total kidney volume (TKV) and Mayo imaging classification (MIC) is essential for assessing disease severity in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). This study aimed to develop and validate a deep learning-based method using noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scans to automate TKV measurement and MIC assignment. Materials and methods A retrospective dataset of 60 ADPKD patients was used to train a three-dimensional (3D) UNet model for kidney segmentation and TKV estimation. Kidney axes were calculated using principal component analysis (PCA). The model was tested on consecutive scans from 30 patients (median interval: 3.6 years) and 28 external patient scans. Segmentation accuracy was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), and measurement reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). MIC was assigned and compared across timepoints. Results The model achieved high segmentation accuracy (DSC: 0.93 ± 0.04 [mean ± standard deviation] and 0.94 ± 0.03 for consecutive scans; 0.96 ± 0.08 for external validation). Manual and automated TKV measurements were strongly correlated (ICC: 0.94-0.99, p < 0.001), with a mean volume error of 7.61 ± 7.26%. MIC assignment matched in 90-93.3% of cases. Kidney dimensions (length > 16.5 cm, width > 9.5 cm, depth > 8 cm) predicted high-risk MIC classes with positive predictive values > 88%. Longitudinal analysis showed significant increases in TKV and declines in estimated glomerular filtration rate-eGFR (p < 0.001). Conclusion The proposed method enables accurate TKV quantification and MIC classification from noncontrast CT, supporting severity assessment and longitudinal monitoring in ADPKD. The proposed method enables accurate TKV quantification and MIC classification from noncontrast CT, supporting severity assessment and longitudinal monitoring in ADPKD.

title: Combining shear wave elastography and ultrasound localization microscopy for liver fibrosis staging in a rat model.
abstract: Objective Accurate staging of liver fibrosis (LF) remains a clinical challenge. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate the diagnostic value of combining shear wave elastography (SWE) and ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) for LF staging across the full disease spectrum. We sought to integrate liver mechanical properties and microvascular structural parameters to build a multiparametric model for fibrosis staging. Materials and methods LF was induced in Sprague-Dawley rats and histologically staged according to the METAVIR system. A total of 62 rats were included in the final analysis. Both SWE and ULM were performed in each animal. Liver viscoelastic moduli were estimated from SWE data using SW-VEI-Net, a physics-informed neural network-based approach. ULM data were post-processed to reconstruct super-resolution images of the hepatic microvasculature, followed by quantitative analysis to extract microvascular structural parameters. Results Histology revealed fibrosis stages F0 (n = 10), F1 (n = 12), F2 (n = 19), F3 (n = 11), and F4 (n = 10). Compared with the single-modality SWE and ULM models, the multiparametric combined model achieved the highest numerical areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve across the four classification tasks: 0.93 for F0 versus F1-F4, 0.92 for F0-F1 versus F2-F4, 0.90 for F0-F2 versus F3-F4, and 0.89 for F0-F3 versus F4. Conclusion Combining SWE-derived viscoelastic parameters with ULM-derived microvascular features enabled multiparametric characterization of LF in this preclinical rat model. Independent validation in larger animal cohorts and, ultimately, human studies is essential before robust clinical conclusions can be drawn. Key points Question Can combining shear-wave elastography (SWE) and ULM improve the accuracy of LF staging? Findings By integrating viscoelastic and microvascular features, the SWE-ULM combined model achieved the highest numerical AUCs across all four fibrosis classifications in a rat model. Relevance statement The SWE and ULM combined model suggests potential value for LF staging by integrating viscoelastic and microvascular biomarkers, providing a basis for further investigation toward future clinical translation.

title: Radiomics performance to identify high-risk carotid artery plaques: a systematic review.
abstract: Background Stroke is a leading cause of mortality worldwide, with 15-20% of ischemic strokes caused by extracranial carotid atherosclerotic disease. Risk stratification has traditionally relied on luminal stenosis severity, which inadequately reflects plaque vulnerability. Radiomics offers an emerging solution by extracting high-dimensional quantitative data from standard medical images. This systematic review evaluated the performance of radiomics-based models for identifying high-risk carotid plaques. Materials and methods A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases. Studies were included if they developed or validated radiomics-based models for carotid plaque assessment and reported performance metrics, specifically the area under the curve (AUC). Data were extracted on study design, imaging modalities, segmentation methods, and modeling techniques. Results Twenty-eight studies involving 6,108 patients (72.4% male) were included. Computed tomography angiography was the most commonly used imaging modality (n = 16), and manual region-of-interest segmentation was performed in 27 of 28 studies. Radiomics models showed strong predictive performance. Internal validation AUCs were as high as 0.984, whereas combined models incorporating radiomics with clinical and/or conventional radiological features achieved the best predictive accuracy, often exceeding 0.90. However, only four studies included external validation cohorts. Conclusion Radiomics is a powerful, non-invasive tool for identifying high-risk carotid plaques, offering superior discriminative power over conventional stenosis-based assessments. Despite these promising results, the field faces significant hurdles, and future research must prioritize prospective multicenter trials, the development of automated segmentation workflows, and the correlation of radiomic features with histopathological findings to ensure clinical reproducibility and transition into routine stroke prevention. Key points Question Standard carotid atherosclerotic disease assessments fail to capture biological plaque complexity and vulnerability, necessitating objective, reproducible, and non-invasive methods to improve stroke prevention. Findings Radiomics and combined models demonstrate superior capability in identifying high-risk carotid plaques compared to traditional assessments. With four external validations, the field remains exploratory. Relevance statement Radiomics offers a non-invasive tool for personalized stroke prevention. However, technical barriers currently prevent its transition to routine clinical use, including reliance on manual segmentation and low compliance with international standardization guidelines.

title: Radiomics-based risk prediction: survival in sarcopenic gastrointestinal and genitourinary cancer cohorts using a population-specific sarcopenia definition.
abstract: Objective This study demonstrated that the recently proposed Asian (Japanese)-cohort-based skeletal muscle index (SMI) definition (< 36.2 cm2/m2 for males and < 29.6 cm2/m2 for females), along with other factors such as radiomic and clinical variables, could improve risk categorization for survival in sarcopenic, gastrointestinal (GI), and genitourinary (GU) cancer patients. Materials and methods This retrospective study involved 2,015 patients who underwent major surgery at our institution between 2006 and 2018. From the axial CT image of the L3 vertebral region, the skeletal muscle was segmented to calculate the SMI values. 646 radiomic features were extracted from the image, and the Boruta algorithm was used to identify the most pertinent features. The final set of features consisted of these features and clinical variables. The dataset was split into training and testing sets comprising 1,512 patients (75%) and 503 patients (25%), respectively. Four models were evaluated in this study: (1) random survival forest (RSF)-based radiomic model, (2) Cox proportional hazard-based model, (3) Asian (Japanese)-specific SMI definition-based model, and (4) integrated model, which combines experiments (2) and (3). The Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves, log-rank tests, and Harrell's concordance index (C-index) were computed to assess the predictive performance of the models. Results The integrated model achieved the highest performance in terms of C-index (0.760, 95% CI: 0.686-0.835) among all other models. Survival stratification was statistically significant across all the experiments (p < 0.0001). Conclusion This work demonstrates the efficacy of utilizing recently proposed Japanese population-based SMI definition values to optimize risk stratification for sarcopenic patients. Key points Question Can population-specific sarcopenia definitions, clinical variables, and CT muscle radiomics together improve overall survival risk stratification in patients with gastrointestinal and genitourinary cancers? Findings In this cohort of 2,015 patients, combining sarcopenia, clinical variables, and CT muscle radiomics yielded an overall survival C-index of 0.760. Relevance statement The incorporation of the Asian (Japanese)-specific skeletal muscle index definition improves risk stratification for the survival of sarcopenic cancer patients when combined with an imaging-based approach, such as radiomics and other clinical parameters, highlighting the value of multimodal integration.

title: Optimizing the contrast agent dose and image acquisition time for renal ultrasound localization microscopy.
abstract: Objective Renal microvascular assessment is essential for kidney function. Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) enables super-resolution imaging of renal microvasculature. However, contrast dose and acquisition time need to be optimized. This study explored the effects of contrast agent dose and acquisition time on renal cortical microvascular imaging. Materials and methods In this prospective study, healthy volunteers underwent renal contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) using four sulfur hexafluoride microbubbles doses (0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.2 mL). ULM was performed during cortical (peak enhancement), medullary, and delayed phases. Quantitative CEUS perfusion parameters and ULM-derived microvascular metrics were assessed, and the effects of dose and time were evaluated using repeated-measures ANOVA. The minimal effective dose was predefined using repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni correction as the lowest dose without significant benefit from higher doses. Results Twenty-five participants were included. CEUS parameters, including area under the curve, peak intensity, half-time to peak, and acceleration time, demonstrated a clear dose-response relationship, plateauing at doses ≥ 0.6 mL (all p ≤ 0.008). ULM imaging was most favorable during the peak enhancement phase. Four distinct patterns of ULM parameters were identified: dose- and time-dependent, dose-dependent, time-dependent, and stable. Among these, the dose- and time-dependent parameters (e.g., vessel ratio, maximum velocity, mean velocity) exhibited the most consistent plateau at 0.6 mL, paralleling the CEUS findings. Conclusion In healthy, non-obese adults, a 0.6-mL dose at peak enhancement reached a plateau in quantitative performance and may represent a practical minimal effective protocol for renal ULM. Key points Question What are the optimal contrast dose and acquisition time for renal ULM protocols, given that they are not currently standardized? Findings A minimal effective dose of 0.6 mL at peak enhancement in healthy, non-obese adults was found. Multiparametric ULM shows good to excellent intra- and inter-observer repeatability for protocol optimization. Relevance statement Renal ULM enables quantitative assessment of cortical microvascular perfusion. This technique provides a reference for optimizing contrast dose and acquisition time, supporting standardized imaging protocols for kidney function evaluation.

title: Multiparametric 0.4-T low-field MRI mapping for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in rats.
abstract: Objective Low-field MRI may broaden access to quantitative liver imaging, but low signal-to-noise ratio and coexisting steatosis, inflammation, fibrosis, and iron complicate relaxometry in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). We evaluated multiparametric 0.4-T MRI with deep-learning-reconstructed T1 mapping in rats. Materials and methods In this prospective cross-sectional preclinical study, 90 male Wistar rats underwent 0.4-T liver MRI during dietary induction, progression, and recovery. Metrics included native T1, fat-corrected T1 (FcT1), T2, T2 * , and an apparent proton density fat fraction (PDFF) estimate. Whole-section digital pathology quantified steatosis, fibrosis, inflammation, and iron. Associations were assessed using iron-adjusted and stage-aware analyses, multivariable regression with variance inflation factors, and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results Steatosis strongly correlated with T2 (ρ = 0.90, p < 0.001) and PDFF (ρ = 0.88, p < 0.001). For high inflammation, T2 and T2 * yielded areas under the curve (AUROCs) of 0.86 (95% confidence interval 0.78-0.94) and 0.80 (0.71-0.89), respectively (p = 0.294); specificities were 82.2% and 91.1%, respectively. For fibrosis, native T1 yielded higher AUROCs than FcT1 at collagen proportionate area (CPA) > 2.42% (0.77 versus 0.62; p = 0.008) and > 2.90% (0.78 versus 0.60; p = 0.001). Stage-aware analyses attenuated T1-fibrosis associations, and recovery animals showed residual fibrosis with near-baseline T1. Conclusion Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI showed complementary, partly stage-dependent associations with MASLD pathology. T2/PDFF tracked steatosis; T2 * retained an inflammation-related association after stage adjustment; and T1 elevation characterized active high-burden progression rather than isolated residual fibrosis. Human validation and platform calibration are required. Key points Question Noninvasive MASLD assessment needs accessible imaging biomarkers that account for coexisting steatosis, inflammation, fibrosis, and iron-related confounding in liver MRI. Findings Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI showed complementary but stage-dependent associations: T2/apparent PDFF tracked steatosis, T2 * related to inflammation, and T1 rose during high-burden progression. Relevance statement Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI provides complementary pathology-correlated measurements for MASLD assessment in rats, but reconstruction-dependent T1 bias and apparent PDFF estimation require platform calibration and human validation before clinical interpretation.

T2/PDFF tracked steatosis; T2* retained an inflammation-related association after stage adjustment; and T1 elevation characterized active high-burden progression rather than isolated residual fibrosis. Human validation and platform calibration are required.

Key points

Question Noninvasive MASLD assessment needs accessible imaging biomarkers that account for coexisting steatosis, inflammation, fibrosis, and iron-related confounding in liver MRI. Findings Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI showed complementary but stage-dependent associations: T2/apparent PDFF tracked steatosis, T2* related to inflammation, and T1 rose during high-burden progression. Relevance statement Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI provides complementary pathology-correlated measurements for MASLD assessment in rats, but reconstruction-dependent T1 bias and apparent PDFF estimation require platform calibration and human validation before clinical interpretation.

title: Central and peripheral Neurolymphomatosis, a rare involvement of DLBCL on PET/CT.
abstract: In this paper we present two rare cases of patients suffering from diffuse large B-cell lymphoma initially treated with chemotherapy. During follow-up, they presented with central and peripheral neurological symptoms, respectively. On PET/CT, intense uptake of FDG was seen indicating neurolymphomatosis. Because of the localization it was not possible to take a biopsy for histological examination, but clinicians relied on imaging, clinical course and laboratory tests for a final diagnosis. Both patients died shortly after this examination underlining the poor prognosis of neurolymphomatosis.

title: ⁶⁸Ga-FAPI PET/CT in cardiac Anderson-Fabry disease: novel insights into disease assessment from a case series.
abstract: Anderson-Fabry disease (AFD) is an X-linked lysosomal disorder in which cardiac involvement is the main cause of morbidity and mortality, manifesting as left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, arrhythmias, and myocardial fibrosis. Myocardial fibrosis is a key pathophysiological process associated with an adverse prognosis. While cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) identifies established myocardial fibrosis, fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI) PET enables the molecular assessment of FAP-associated activity. By complementing conventional CMR parameters, including late gadolinium enhancement and native T1 mapping, FAPI PET may improve the characterization and phenotypic classification of cardiac involvement in Anderson-Fabry disease. We report three cases of AFD patients, who underwent Gallium-68-fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (⁶⁸Ga-FAPI) PET-CT as part of a prospective study designed to assess myocardial fibrosis. Overall, ⁶⁸Ga-FAPI uptake closely correlated with CMR findings, reinforcing the role of cardiac fibroblast activation as a relevant pathogenic mechanism in AFD. These findings highlight this new molecular imaging as a promising tool for early detection, risk stratification, and therapeutic guidance in AFD.

title: Clinical evaluation of a novel artificial intelligence-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiography.
abstract: Background To evaluate the clinical performance of a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiographic imaging compared with its predecessor across multiple imaging modes, anatomic regions, and endovascular specialties. Materials and methods This retrospective, comparative, randomized, paired, and blinded multicenter reader study included anonymized images acquired during clinically indicated endovascular interventions at 11 institutions in the United States and Europe. A total of 553 image series from 182 patients representing 51 procedure types across interventional radiology, neurointervention, cardiology, and pediatric cardiology were processed using both the AI-based and predecessor image processing algorithms. Thirteen board-certified physicians independently evaluated paired images using five-point Likert scales for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details. The primary endpoint was non-inferiority of overall image quality. Secondary endpoints evaluated superiority across image quality metrics using a predefined hierarchical testing strategy. Results The AI-based image processing algorithm demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality in 98.9% of all evaluations (95% confidence interval [CI], 98%-100%), meeting the primary endpoint across all imaging modes, anatomic regions, and predefined subgroups. Superiority of the AI-based algorithm was demonstrated for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details across fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. Overall image quality superiority was not demonstrated for digital subtraction angiography, likely reflecting the intrinsically higher signal-to-noise characteristics of these acquisitions. Inter-reader agreement analysis demonstrated identical ratings in 49.3% of evaluations, with 94.7% of paired ratings differing by no more than one Likert category. Conclusions In this multicenter blinded reader study, AI-based image processing demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality compared with its predecessor across all evaluated imaging modes and patient subgroups, with superior performance for multiple image quality metrics in fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. These findings support the clinical utility of AI-based image processing for endovascular imaging and provide a foundation for future studies evaluating its impact on radiation dose and procedural outcomes.

title: Portable endovascular disposable robotic assistant (PEDRA) for image-guided peripheral endovascular interventions: technical feasibility, safety, and future implications.
abstract: Background Traditional fixed-console endovascular robots face barriers due to high capital costs and infrastructure requirements. This study evaluates the technical feasibility and safety of the LIBERTY® Endovascular Robotic System-a portable, disposable platform-across diverse Interventional Radiology procedures and vascular access sites. Materials and methods A single-center retrospective review was conducted on 20 consecutive outpatient procedures performed by five operators. Cases included prostate artery embolization, uterine fibroid embolization, renal/gonadal venography, geniculate artery embolization, Y90 mapping, and Y90 radioembolization. Vascular access points included left radial and femoral approaches. Results Procedural technical success was achieved in 100% (20/20) of cases. 100% of vessels attempted with robotic assistance were successfully selected (31/31). Complete robotic target-vessel selection-performing all procedural aspects of vessel selection robotically-was 75% (15/20). Partial robotic target-vessel selection-conversion to manual prior to completion of all vessel selections with robotic assistance-was 25% (5/20). All 5 cases of partial robotic target-vessel selection were due to hardware malfunction, rather than an inability to select target vessels with robotic assistance. Subgroup analysis of the last 10 cases after switching to utilizing updated units demonstrated 100% complete robotic target-vessel selection (10/10). No device-related serious adverse events or complications occurred. Conclusion The portable and disposable robotic platform was successfully integrated into a diverse Interventional Radiology practice, demonstrating the first documented prostate artery embolization, uterine fibroid embolization, renal/gonadal venography, geniculate artery embolization, and Y90 procedures by portable and disposable robotic-assistance, as well as the first robotic-assisted endovascular procedures via radial access. Its design may lower economic and institutional barriers, potentially expanding robotic-assisted interventions to rural or non-academic settings. The portable robotic assistant is safe and feasible for complex endovascular interventions. Further prospective studies are needed to quantify ergonomic benefits and radiation reduction.

title: Characteristics of ischemic stroke patients with left atrial appendage thrombus detected by cardiac photon-counting detector computed tomography.
abstract: Background The early identification of left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombus in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) or transient ischemic attack (TIA) patients can have relevant treatment and prognostic implications. We investigated the prevalence of LAA thrombus in AIS/TIA patients and analyzed baseline characteristics and short-term outcomes according to the presence of LAA thrombus. Methods We analyzed stroke patients who were admitted consecutively in our comprehensive stroke centre between March 2023 and December 2025 and received cardiac photon-counting computed tomography (CT) implemented in the acute stroke imaging protocol. We analyzed baseline clinical characteristics, echocardiographic and laboratory biomarkers, in-hospital mortality and in-hospital ischemic stroke recurrence according to the presence of LAA thrombus. Results We included 577 patients with a median age of 75 years, 49.6% were female, and LAA thrombus was found in 49 patients (8.5%). The presence of LAA thrombus was independently associated with atrial fibrillation (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 16.09, 95% confidence interval [95%CI] = 4.55-56.90, p < 0.001), severe left atrial dilatation (aOR = 3.48, 95%CI = 1.18-10.26, p = 0.009) and higher NT-proBNP (aOR per 1000pg/mL-increment = 1.10, 95%CI = 1.01-1.19, p = 0.022). In-hospital mortality was higher in patients with LAA thrombus (p = 0.003), but this association did not persist after adjustment for clinical stroke severity. In-hospital ischemic stroke recurrence was similar in both groups. Conclusions Stroke patients with LAA thrombus detected on cardiac CT performed as part of the acute stroke imaging protocol have different baseline characteristics which are indicative of more severe underlying atrial substrate for arrhythmogenesis.

title: Enhanced multi-object detection in brachial plexus ultrasound images using transformer-based semantic and spatial feature fusion.
abstract: Advances in medical imaging have led to the widespread use of ultrasound for diagnosing and treating peripheral nerve blocks. However, challenges such as speckle noise and low spatial resolution hinder the accurate identification of neural structures. To address these issues, a model named transformer-based detection with semantic and spatial feature fusion (TDSS) was introduced, integrating spatial edge adaptive enhancement, multi-scale semantic fusion, and spatial distillation-assisted detection modules. These components improve edge perception, multi-scale semantic reasoning, and localization accuracy. Experiments on the Ultrasound Brachial Plexus Dataset demonstrated the superior performance of the model: TDSS achieved an AP of 0.407 for nerve detection and an overall mAP of 0.583, providing robust support for clinical medical image detection. The source code for the proposed TDSS framework is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18824199 .

title: Smartwatch-based pelvic tracking system for augmented reality navigation in total hip arthroplasty: a preliminary clinical study.
abstract: Background Accurate assessment of pelvic orientation is essential for acetabular cup placement during total hip arthroplasty (THA). Conventional pelvic tracking systems generally rely on dedicated tracking hardware and optical tracking infrastructure. We developed a smartwatch-based pelvic tracking system integrated with an augmented reality (AR) navigation platform and evaluated its preliminary clinical performance. Methods This retrospective study included 30 hips of 27 consecutive patients who underwent primary THA using a smartwatch-based pelvic tracking navigation system between May 2025 and April 2026. The system utilizes a commercially available smartwatch fixed to the iliac crest as a pelvic tracking device and communicates orientation information to a smartphone-based AR navigation platform via Bluetooth. Acetabular cup orientation was evaluated using postoperative CT. Absolute radiographic inclination (RI) and anteversion (RA) errors were calculated as absolute differences between the final intraoperative navigation measurements and postoperative CT measurements. Results The mean absolute RI error was 2.8° ± 2.1°, and the mean absolute RA error was 3.6° ± 2.2°. Postoperative CT measurements were within 5° of the final intraoperative navigation measurements for RI and RA in 86.7% and 70.0% of hips, respectively. Navigation was successfully completed in all 30 hips, with no conversion to a backup technique. Additional bench testing demonstrated reproducible smartwatch reattachment and reduction of time-dependent relative orientation differences following FPP invocation. Conclusions This study demonstrated the feasibility of integrating a commercially available smartwatch into a pelvic tracking system for THA navigation. The smartwatch-based pelvic tracking platform achieved a preliminary range of cup-positioning accuracy without requiring continuous optical visualization of a pelvic reference marker while utilizing a compact and widely available consumer wearable device. This study represents the first step toward wearable-device-based navigation in arthroplasty.

Accurate assessment of pelvic orientation is essential for acetabular cup placement during total hip arthroplasty (THA). Conventional pelvic tracking systems generally rely on dedicated tracking hardware and optical tracking infrastructure. We developed a smartwatch-based pelvic tracking system integrated with an augmented reality (AR) navigation platform and evaluated its preliminary clinical performance.

Methods

This retrospective study included 30 hips of 27 consecutive patients who underwent primary THA using a smartwatch-based pelvic tracking navigation system between May 2025 and April 2026. The system utilizes a commercially available smartwatch fixed to the iliac crest as a pelvic tracking device and communicates orientation information to a smartphone-based AR navigation platform via Bluetooth. Acetabular cup orientation was evaluated using postoperative CT. Absolute radiographic inclination (RI) and anteversion (RA) errors were calculated as absolute differences between the final intraoperative navigation measurements and postoperative CT measurements.

Results

The mean absolute RI error was 2.8° ± 2.1°, and the mean absolute RA error was 3.6° ± 2.2°. Postoperative CT measurements were within 5° of the final intraoperative navigation measurements for RI and RA in 86.7% and 70.0% of hips, respectively. Navigation was successfully completed in all 30 hips, with no conversion to a backup technique. Additional bench testing demonstrated reproducible smartwatch reattachment and reduction of time-dependent relative orientation differences following FPP invocation.

Conclusions

This study demonstrated the feasibility of integrating a commercially available smartwatch into a pelvic tracking system for THA navigation. The smartwatch-based pelvic tracking platform achieved a preliminary range of cup-positioning accuracy without requiring continuous optical visualization of a pelvic reference marker while utilizing a compact and widely available consumer wearable device. This study represents the first step toward wearable-device-based navigation in arthroplasty.

title: Distinguishing artificial intelligence from robotic execution in total knee arthroplasty: a narrative review and evidence map.
abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning methods are increasingly discussed in relation to robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA). However, robotic assistance, computer navigation, and AI-based prediction represent distinct functions that are often conflated under the single label "AI-assisted robotic TKA," obscuring the state of evidence for each. This review clarifies these distinctions and maps the current evidence for AI-related functions across the TKA pathway, keeping AI prediction evidence analytically separate from robotic execution evidence at the level of each clinical function. Methods We performed a critical narrative review and evidence map of peer-reviewed literature relevant to robotic-assisted TKA, navigation-assisted TKA, AI/ML prediction models, digital planning, implant sizing, intraoperative decision support, postoperative monitoring, implementation, and economic evaluation. Evidence was interpreted according to clinical function, comparator structure, validation status, and translational maturity. Because the available literature is methodologically and conceptually heterogeneous, quantitative pooling and formal comparative-effectiveness claims were not attempted. Results Robotic-assisted and navigation-assisted TKA have the most mature evidence base for improving technical precision, particularly implant positioning and radiographic alignment. In contrast, AI/ML evidence is concentrated mainly in adjacent pathway functions, including radiographic interpretation, implant-sizing prediction, patient-selection support, dissatisfaction prediction, outcome modelling, perioperative risk stratification, and postoperative monitoring. Direct clinical evidence demonstrating that AI-enabled robotic TKA provides incremental patient-level benefit beyond conventional robotic assistance remains limited. Current studies are constrained by inconsistent terminology, short follow-up, limited external validation, incomplete reporting of AI components, heterogeneous outcomes, cost uncertainty, and uncertain generalizability across patient populations and healthcare settings. Conclusion AI should not currently be treated as a single validated surgical intervention in TKA. Rather, it represents a family of emerging pathway-level functions that may support preoperative planning, intraoperative decision support, patient selection, risk communication, and longitudinal recovery monitoring. Future studies should explicitly define the AI component being evaluated, distinguish AI functionality from robotic or navigation assistance, use standardized comparators, and assess long-term patient-reported outcomes, implant survivorship, safety, cost-effectiveness, and equity across multicenter prospective cohorts or randomized trials.

title: Longitudinal changes in infrapatellar fat pad fibrosis following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Background Infrapatellar fat pad (IFP) fibrosis is implicated in anterior knee pain, limited range of motion (ROM), and posttraumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). However, its precise longitudinal progression remains unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the dynamic changes in IFP fibrosis from preoperative to 12 months post-ACLR using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Methods We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients who underwent anatomic double-bundle ACLR using autologous hamstring tendon grafts. IFP fibrosis was semiquantitatively graded (grades 0-5) using proton density-weighted (PDW) sagittal MR images obtained preoperatively and at 6 and 12 months postoperatively. Patients were categorized into mild (grades 0-3) and severe (grades 4-5) IFP fibrosis groups. Temporal changes in the proportion of the severe group across the three time points were evaluated using Cochran's Q test, followed by the Bonferroni-corrected McNemar test for pairwise comparisons. Results Of 558 consecutive cases screened, 169 patients (mean age, 23.9 years) were included in the final analysis. The proportion of patients classified into the severe fibrosis group significantly changed over time (Cochran's Q test, χ 2 (2) = 24.0, p < 0.001). Compared with the preoperative proportion (1.2%), the proportion of patients in the severe group increased significantly at 6 months postoperatively (8.3%, p = 0.003) and persisted at 12 months (8.3%, p = 0.003). Crucially, 91.1% of the patients showed no change in fibrosis grade between 6 and 12 months. This demonstrates that IFP fibrosis significantly progressed within the first 6 months post-ACLR, with minimal subsequent changes up to 12 months. Conclusions IFP fibrosis is an early and persistent pathological event following ACLR and is established primarily within the first 6 postoperative months. This early onset suggests a critical time window for targeted interventions to mitigate inflammation and prevent the irreversible establishment of IFP fibrosis, providing a basis to investigate the long-term PTOA risk.

title: Treatment of Stage IB to III Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: CSCO-ASCO Guideline Update.
abstract: Purpose To update the 2021 CSCO-ASCO guideline on chemotherapy in combination with radiotherapy for the definitive treatment of non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), incorporating new evidence on radiotherapy techniques and target-volume de-escalation, chemotherapy regimens and their sequencing, adjuvant therapy, and immunotherapy for patients with stage IB-III disease. Methods A multidisciplinary Expert Panel reviewed evidence published since the prior guideline, including randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant prospective and retrospective studies. Outcomes of interest included overall survival, failure-free or progression-free survival, locoregional and distant disease control, acute and late toxicities, and patient-reported quality of life. Recommendations were developed using the ASCO guideline development process and Expert Panel consensus. Results The updated evidence supports: IMRT with image guidance and MRI-based target delineation as core components of definitive treatment; selected response-adapted target delineation following induction chemotherapy; elective nodal de-escalation in appropriately selected patients; risk-adapted chemotherapy sequencing according to stage and biologic risk; cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy; gemcitabine-cisplatin (GP) or docetaxel-cisplatin-fluorouracil (TPF) as preferred induction regimens; and selected adjuvant chemotherapy options, including metronomic capecitabine for patients with higher residual post-chemoradiotherapy risk. Several randomized trials evaluating PD-1 inhibitors have demonstrated improved disease-control outcomes, but overall survival data remain immature. Recommendations This guideline update provides recommendations on radiotherapy technique, dose, imaging, and target delineation; sequencing of additional chemotherapy with radiotherapy; concurrent chemotherapy options; induction chemotherapy regimens and timing; adjuvant chemotherapy options; and the role of immunotherapy. At present, the Panel makes no recommendation for or against routine addition of immunotherapy to induction-concurrent chemoradiotherapy; applicability of the trial evidence, benefits and harms, local approval and access, and patient preferences should guide individualized decisions.Additional information is available at www.ascopubs.org/topics/asco-guidelines/head-neck-cancer.

title: Interventional Oncology in Oligometastatic Disease: Closing the Treatment Gap.
abstract: Metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) is currently an increasingly established component of oligometastatic disease (OMD) management. Interventional radiology (IR) offers a broad range of image-guided MDT options, including thermal ablation, nonthermal ablation, and transarterial therapies, yet remains structurally underutilized within multidisciplinary treatment pathways. As a result, IR-delivered therapies are often evaluated in late-referral or salvage contexts, producing comparative outcome data that are heavily influenced by selection bias and confounding by indication. Interpretation of the IR evidence base is further complicated by evidentiary lag, as many mature outcome data derive from earlier-generation technologies that may not fully reflect contemporary practice. This is particularly important because, in carefully selected patients and in the limited settings where randomized or well-controlled comparative data exist, IR-delivered therapies can achieve oncologic outcomes comparable with more invasive modalities while substantially reducing treatment morbidity, recovery time, hospital stay, and cost. MDT selection in OMD is inherently multidimensional: Durable local control must be weighed against treatment burden, repeatability, preservation of systemic therapy options, logistical feasibility, and patient preference. We summarize the evidence supporting IR-based MDT across hepatic, pulmonary, adrenal, nodal, osseous, and emerging neuro-oncologic OMD sites, with comparison with established surgical and radiotherapeutic approaches. We further propose a Pareto-based conceptual framework for patient-centered modality selection, in which multiple treatment strategies may represent efficient trade-offs rather than a single universally optimal approach. Interventional oncology should be viewed not as a salvage service but as an essential fourth pillar of cancer care alongside medical, surgical, and radiation oncology.

title: Redefining the EPCAM Phenotype: Deletion Architecture Determines Lynch Syndrome Cancer Risk.
abstract: Purpose To characterize the cancer phenotype and clinical presentation across molecularly distinct EPCAM deletion subgroups and determine how the phenotype varies with MSH2 involvement. Methods We retrospectively evaluated 662 unrelated probands undergoing hereditary cancer multigene panel testing (MGPT) with isolated EPCAM full-gene deletions (n = 22), isolated EPCAM 3' deletions (n = 96), contiguous EPCAM full-gene deletions extending into MSH2 (n = 64), contiguous EPCAM 3' deletions extending into MSH2 (n = 116), MSH2 gross deletions (n = 155), and MSH2 nonsense/frameshift (ns/fs) variants (n = 209). Lynch syndrome (LS)-associated cancer prevalence, tumor spectrum, and PREMM5 scores were compared across cohorts. Multivariable logistic regression estimated cancer-specific associations relative to a MGPT-negative reference cohort. Results Isolated EPCAM full-gene deletions, comprising 18.6% of observed isolated EPCAM deletions, were not significantly associated with LS-associated cancers. The LS-associated cancer prevalence was 13.6% in this cohort, compared with 54.6% with isolated EPCAM 3' deletions and 64.1%-72.2% in MSH2 -involving cohorts ( P < .001). Relative to MGPT-negative individuals, isolated EPCAM 3' deletions were strongly associated with colorectal cancer (odds ratio [OR], 17.59; P < .001) but not endometrial cancer (OR, 0.76; P = .790). MSH2 -involving cohorts demonstrated strong associations with both colorectal (ORs, 8.50-16.03; P < .001) and endometrial cancers (ORs, 17.31-30.47; P < .001). Conclusion These findings provide new insights into the molecular and clinical heterogeneity of germline deletions involving EPCAM . Expanded detection across the full EPCAM gene and its 3' region distinguishes isolated full-gene deletions, which do not disrupt downstream MSH2 and are not associated with LS phenotypes, from isolated 3' deletions with a colorectal-predominant phenotype, and contiguous EPCAM-MSH2 deletions with an MSH2 -like LS phenotype. Precise delineation of EPCAM deletion boundaries and MSH2 involvement define three clinically relevant risk groups and support more precise risk assessment, counseling, and surveillance.

title: Sclerosing mucoepidermoid thyroid carcinoma with eosinophilia treated by thyroidectomy and radiotherapy.
abstract: Sclerosing mucoepidermoid carcinoma with eosinophilia (SMECE) is a rare thyroid malignancy with fewer than 100 reported cases. We present a 48-year-old male with dysphagia, fatigue, night sweats, and a 43-pound weight loss over 4 months. Evaluation revealed profound hypothyroidism and a thyroid gland entirely replaced by a hypoechoic mass on ultrasound. Core needle biopsy was nondiagnostic, and the patient underwent total thyroidectomy. Pathology confirmed SMECE involving both lobes, measuring 11.1 cm, with extrathyroidal extension into the surrounding adipose tissue. Given the lack of thyroglobulin expression in SMECE, radioactive iodine was not considered effective, and adjuvant external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) was administered at a dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions. At 18 months of follow-up, the patient remains free of recurrence. Given the absence of management consensus for SMECE, this case highlights the potential role of EBRT in patients with locoregional invasion.

Given the lack of thyroglobulin expression in SMECE, radioactive iodine was not considered effective, and adjuvant external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) was administered at a dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions. At 18 months of follow-up, the patient remains free of recurrence. Given the absence of management consensus for SMECE, this case highlights the potential role of EBRT in patients with locoregional invasion.

title: International Multicenter Retrospective Study on UBTF -Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
abstract: Background and objectives UBTF encodes the upstream binding transcription factor (UBTF), a protein essential for rRNA synthesis. Dominantly acting pathogenic variants, either de novo or inherited, have been associated with a broad clinical childhood-onset neurodegenerative/neurodevelopmental spectrum whose genotype-phenotype correlation has not been accurately defined yet. This multicenter study aims to conduct a retrospective analysis of a large cohort of patients with pathogenic variants in the UBTF gene to refine diagnostic criteria and identify clinically relevant outcome measures for future trials. Methods Clinical centers provided clinical, molecular, and neuroimaging data on patients carrying pathogenic or predicted pathogenic UBTF variants, consistent with the clinical phenotype. Data were collected using an human phenotype ontology-based standardized electronic case report form and included unreported cases or updated information on patients reported in the literature from January 2017 to December 2024. Results A cohort of 49 patients (23 previously unreported) was included in the study. The disease typically presented at ≤3 years (89.6%) with neuroregression in 71.4% of cases, either in a child with preexisting neurodevelopmental delay (42.9%) or after previously normal psychomotor development (28.6%). Less frequently, neurodevelopmental delay occurred in isolation (26.5%). During disease progression, patients developed behavioral abnormalities (81.6%), movement disorders (78.3%), autonomic manifestations (50.0%), and epilepsy (34.7%). At the last follow-up (mean age 13 years and 6 months), only 2 patients were deceased (4.1%). The main neuroimaging findings included white matter hyperintensity (68.1%), cerebral (66.0%) and cerebellar (51.1%) atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum (38.3%). However, brain MRI findings were reported as normal in 21.3% of cases. We identified 7 novel UBTF variants (c.271G>C; c.349A>T; c.495C>A; c.517G>A; c.761A>G; c.1048-2A>G; and c.1625_1626+15del). Genotype-phenotype analysis led to the distinction of 2 allelic, clinically distinct disorders: a childhood-onset neurodegenerative disease due to gain-of-function variants, characterized by the triad of neuroregression, movement, and behavioral disorders, and a neurodevelopmental disorder with a milder clinical course associated with loss-of-function/hypomorphic variants. Discussion The results from our deep-phenotyping analysis suggest the classification of UBTF -related disease into 2 main clinical syndromes impacting the natural history of the disease with a different degree of severity and complexity. This novel observation should be considered in the management and prognosis of patients and will be fundamental in the design of targeted therapies.
